The plan includes 137 market-rate housing units and 60 low-income housing units, as well as road safety improvements and an expansion to Coaches Field. The City has received over 70 written comments on the Draft Specific Plan since it was released for review in April. articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter After considering its options in response to the Republic Services strike this past summer, and after having requested that Piedmont citizens fill out questionnaires regarding the lack of garbage pickups for one to two weeks, the City has decided on a course of action: do nothing. According to Deniz Ergun, the city’s Sustainability Manager, the City Council did not make a formal decision on the matter. Rather, the course of action is more of a “we’ve talked to other cities affected and no one is doing anything either” sort of thing. She told me that individual customers affected by the strike – in other words, the owners of the 3,737 single family residences in the city – call Republic Services directly to negotiate a credit. However, a random, unscientific check showed that other cities were indeed taking actions on behalf of their residents. The City Manager’s Office in Richmond told this reporter that right after the strike was settled, the City sent a formal letter to Republic requesting a citywide credit for missed services. While Richmond has not yet resolved the matter, they assured me that this was an ongoing matter and would not simply be dropped or ignored. The Daly City Utilities Billing Department told me that credits had already been issued to residential customers. I have left messages with other cities’ Public Works Departments and am waiting for their responses. So why didn’t Piedmont do the same? As usual, the devil is in the details. Speaking with the Customer Service Manager at Republic Services, I learned that Piedmont has a different kind of contract than other cities. Absent force majeure, Republic is required to provide us with contracted services. So, according to them, management personnel staffed the trucks and did the Piedmont routes. In fact, Republic thinks that everyone in Piedmont had their garbage and recycling picked up during the strike. articles.text: City Council heard a proposal to update Planning & Building permit fees and adopted a formal cost recovery policy at their regular meeting on Monday, September 15, 2025, adjusting building permit fees with attention to a residential solar panel rebate program. New permit fees will go into effect January 1, 2026. The proposed updates follow a fee study conducted earlier this year. The study found that current fees only recover 73% of the cost of permit services, resulting in an under-recovery of more than $400,000 per year. Main cost drivers are staff salaries and benefits, departmental and citywide overhead (admin, IT, HR, legal, facilities) and increased complexity of reviews, especially large construction projects. “Best practices include the preparation of fee studies every five years so that the City can evaluate the cost of providing the departments’ services and adjust the fees accordingly,” said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “The intent is to give confidence to property owners, contractors, architects, City staff and decision makers that the fees are rightsized and fair.” Alongside the fee updates, the Council adopted a formal policy documenting that the City’s goal is to set Planning & Building fees at 100% cost recovery, with exceptions when a defined community benefit justifies a subsidy – such as potential reduced fees for residential solar permits as a way to support Piedmont’s climate action goals. City Council directed the Planning Department to move forward with a suggestion to subsidize solar panels through rebates or a reduced cost. The proposed subsidy for residential solar permits would be paid for with a fund of $50,000 set aside as part of the City’s budget. Though some prices are decreasing, the majority of permit fees are raising in price. In some cases, such as with SB9 Housing Development permits, fees can rise by as much as $7,600. Proposed updates include: • Revised fee schedule: Most permit fees would increase to better reflect staff time and resources, while some obsolete fees would be eliminated. • New and expanded categories: New fees would • • be added to reflect recent changes in State law. Certain existing fees, such as solar permits, would be expanded into separate categories for residential and commercial projects. Added valuation tiers: Two new valuation tiers would be created for very large construction projects ($10 million and $25 million), scaling fees proportionally with the complexity of review. Flat-fee conversions: Many common building permits (such as water heaters, HVAC systems, and EV chargers) would be converted from valuation-based to flat fees, making costs more predictable and aligned with the service provided. After adoption, the new fee schedule would take effect on January 1, 2026. The fee study was initiated by the City Council during the FY24-25 budget process, along with an organizational assessment presented earlier this year. These reviews aim to strengthen the Planning & Building Department’s capacity to provide service to the community. So, if someone says they did not get service, it can be verified by comparing their address with the GPS tracking from the trucks. However, this does require every customer who did not receive the contracted services to individually call Republic to request a credit. As a long-time computer geek, I suggested that Republic download its GPS results and use a spreadsheet or database to electronically compare the GPS results to the list of streets in Piedmont, thereby determining the streets that were missed, and then automatically generating credits to affected customers. The reaction I received was the audio equivalent of a deer in the headlights. So, if you didn’t receive your normal service during the strike, you need to call Republic at 800- 320-8077 and let them know. Do it while it is fresh in your mind and before September 30th bills are generated. “Ask and you will receive”, because the City will not do it for you. Finally, we do need to ask why Piedmont decided to sweep this matter under the rug, especially after asking residents to fill out online questionnaires (remember them?) about service levels during the strike. City personnel certainly must have known that streets were missed based on the input from residents. Perhaps they chose to accept Republic’s assertion that there were no service disruptions, or perhaps they simply chose the path requiring the least effort. In any case, they had a responsibility to notify residents, either on the Piedmont website, via the Piedmont Post, or with some other sort of communication. It is disappointing that they chose not to do so.

There will be snacks, giveaways, a raffle, and meetyour-neighbors bingo. Piedmont Community Center will host the Edibles Contest and display the many entries, including produce, prepared dishes and baked goods, and products of the bountiful gardens and creative kitchens of Piedmont. Anyone who lives or works in the City of Piedmont may submit an entry; group entries are allowed and up to four entries may be made per category. To enter the contest, bring a labeled item and entry form to Community Hall between 7:30 and 10:00 a.m. Founded in 1998 by Bill Drum and Susan Hill, the contest now has 27 categories, including: best curds and butters, pies, pesto, most unusual vegetable and three categories for baked bread. Entries will be gauged by a panel of judges composed of city council members, city staff, and various volunteers. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, September 17, 2025 Local Items Adoptable Dog of the Week By Jessica McDevitt Amazon is a dog with a big heart currently in a medium-sized package. At 44-pounds and 8-months-old, this playful Doberman Pinscher/Mixed Breed has been the star of his shelter playgroups where he loves zooming around with his friends in games of chase. articles.text: Piedmont residents meet officers and admire impressive cars at last year’s Cops, Coffee and Car show. The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 7th annual car show, complete with hot coffee and even hotter automobiles this Saturday, September 20, from 9:00 a.m. to noon near the Exedra. The event brings cops, coffee and cars to the center of Piedmont as a part of the department’s outreach efforts. Excitement is revving up as nearly 100 vehicles have been entered in this year’s event. Officer Tyler Petit, organizer of the car show, anticipates more than 120 unique cars to be on display this year. To accommodate the growing turnout, the event will expand from the Community Center parking lot down Magnolia Avenue to the base of Piedmont High School. This year’s car will be an opportunity for Piedmont residents to meet the city’s new Police Chief, Frederick Shavies, along with members of the police department. Along with the impressive lineup of classic and custom vehicles, a taco truck will be on-site. The Cops, Coffee and Car Show was pioneered by former Piedmont Police Sergeant Steve DeWarns in collaboration with Officer Petit in 2018. In its second year, the car show had 44 cars in 2019, and since then has had approximately 100 showroom worthy cars since 2021. To enter a vehicle in the show, e-mail officer Tyler Petit at coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. Be sure to include your name, phone number and e-mail address, and the name, make, model and year of the vehicle. articles.text: Tommy is a 1-year-old gray tabby with bright green eyes and a curious, playful spirit. He’s looking for a calm, indoor-only home with an easygoing feline friend. Although Tommy starts off shy with new people and startles at sudden sounds or movements, he’ll come out of his shell with patience and a slow approach — and that’s when his playful side shines! When you go at his pace, you’ll be rewarded by the cutest antics: this sweet boy loves scampering after wand toys with tassels and gently wrestling with his cat buddies! Your heart will melt when you see how gently he plays, giving headbutts and taking turns “winning.” Tommy can’t resist treats — a great way to earn his trust — and when he feels safe, he enjoys gentle petting in small Meet Tommy at Cat Town. doses. We think he’ll flourish in a home with an adopter with some cat experience who can read his signals. Tommy is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and negative for FeLV and FIV. Want to meet him? articles.text: Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s original unabridged September 8, 2025 Piedmont Pulse is available online at App.smore. com/n/nas4p6 Dear PUSD Families & Staff: As you know, on September 4 an intruder entered the Beach campus by climbing over a fence with the intent to play basketball. While we were fortunate that the individual did not pose a threat beyond making a poor decision, the incident prompted our team and community to reflect on how we can strengthen security and safety measures on our campuses. Our schools have safety plans that outline how we respond to a variety of potential threats. Staff are trained in these protocols, which include close coordination with the Piedmont Police Department (PPD). We also encourage students and community members to follow the “See something, say something” principle to help keep our campuses safe. The recent Beach incident illustrates these protocols in action: when an intruder entered campus, the Principal was immediately notified, the school was placed on lockdown, and PPD arrived within minutes to remove the individual. Thanks to these swift actions, students and staff remained safe throughout the incident. Following this incident, we reviewed our protocols, including feedback from parents, and we will use both the text and email systems to communicate with families when there is a campus emergency. We are also thoughtful about the impact of these events, even when the result is all are safe. Thanks to our School Psychologist, Diana Cooksey for a helpful resource at: Childmind. org/guide/helping-children-copeafter-a-traumatic-event/ for staff and parents. A special thanks to the Beach staff, including the leadership of Principal Anne Valva, for keeping our students safe, along with PPD for their quick response to this safety incident. Finally, thank you to our students and parents for your partnership in safety. In Partnership, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Honoring Chris Stevens As September 11 [passes], we remember those who lost their lives, including Piedmont High School alumnus, Class of 1978, Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens, who dedicated over two decades to the U.S. Foreign Service and was known for his commitment to diplomacy, connection, and democratic ideals. On September 11, 2012, Ambassador Stevens, along with Navy SEALs Glen Doherty and Tyrone Woods and State Department officer Sean Smith, lost their lives during attacks on U.S. facilities in Benghazi, Libya. Their sacrifice highlighted the courage required of those who serve our nation abroad. The loss was felt deeply in Benghazi, where residents mourned Stevens as a trusted friend, and in Piedmont, where our community honored his legacy by naming the high school library the Ambassador Christopher Stevens Memorial Library in 2013 in his memory. His life and service continue to inspire, reflecting the Piedmont High School motto, “Achieve the Honorable.” Learn more about the life of Chris Stevens at: https://out. smore.com/e/nas4p6/XALcm6?__$u__ AC Bus Route Service — Community Advocacy Needed Thank you to the students and parents who took our survey [three] weeks ago and who wrote to AC Transit officials to restore Bus 33 service to upper Piedmont. To those surveyed families, I recently sent out an opportunity to write to AC Transit to restore service. If you would like to join in this letter-writing effort, we could use your help to advocate for this critical transportation need. Linked at: Out.smore.com/e/ nas4p6/RbirFR?__$u__ is information below to assist you in sending a letter via email to the AC Transit staff and Board. We believe advocacy from our PUSD community can make a difference in calling attention to this important matter and potentially leading to the restoration of bus service to upper Piedmont. For high school Juniors and Seniors, this opportunity to advocate locally can earn students the PUSD State Seal of Civic Engagement on a student’s transcript and diploma for college admissions purposes. For Seal Criteria see https://out.smore.com/e/nas4p6/ pLRR4s?__$u__ The AC Transit Board meeting [was] Wednesday, Sept. 10th at 5pm. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich [provided] students dinner and [planned] to meet in Room 30A at PHS to join the AC Transit Board meeting. High School Scheduling During the first several weeks of school, we heard from some parents regarding scheduling issues, including courses that are at capacity and unavailable to students. This moment reminded me of a post I wrote in August 2023 (linked at Out.smore.com/e/ nas4p6/mUaEpc?__$u__) about similar challenges. Two years ago, we experienced uneven enrollment in courses, which prompted me to take a look at the PHS master schedule, in terms of courses offered and how the master schedule of courses was built. Fast-forward to this year, and we experienced similar issues, especially related to courses that are at capacity with no room for additional students. Moreover, two years ago we had approximately 30 additional students over what we have today, with essentially the same courses available to students. One would conclude that we should be able to accommodate most or all of our students’ requests. However, the concerns remain, and we will need to consider more effective ways to build a master schedule of courses for our high school students. Several reasons for the challenges are as follows: TA & Free Periods: Building a student-centered schedule means offering courses they are likely to take. This year, one challenge we faced was the timing of when courses were offered. While our scheduling software is designed to maximize student course preferences, other factors also shape the master schedule, such as the limited number of course sections, teacher availability, and specific course requirements. As a result, some course options during certain periods were less appealing, leading more students at some grade levels to take a TA or free period instead. Although students do not need to take seven classes each year to be admitted to even the most selective colleges, multiple TA (teacher’s assistant) or free “Unscheduled” periods generally do not strengthen a student’s college application, particularly in grades 9–11, unless they supplement their schedule with outside coursework (e.g., a college course). Low Enrollment Courses: Our high school offers a robust catalog of courses. However, some electives attract fewer than 20 students, and in some cases, fewer than 10, which raises questions about sustainability. We also hear from students and families that they sometimes prefer to take courses off campus rather than enroll in certain electives. So, how do we resolve these issues? Two years ago, I shared that while it may seem intuitive to simply add more sections of popular courses so that students can access their top choices, a small high school cannot realistically offer every course during every period. I continue to believe this is true. Therefore, we must be more intentional about the courses we offer, ensuring they align with students’ needs and interests, including a regular review of course requirements that are exclusive to PUSD but not required by the State or as part of the UC A-G requirements. To explore solutions, we will [held] a Board Workshop on September 12 at 1:00 p.m. at the District Office Board Room to discuss options for improving high school course offerings. Courtesy of PUSD PHS classes with low enrollment this fall.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a record-breaking check for $4,116,427 to the Piedmont School Board on Wednesday, September 10. This grant is the largest in the foundation’s history and reflects a full year of fundraising through the Giving Campaign and other programs, such as Spring Fling, Harvest Festival, Dress Best for Less, business sponsorships, and a distribution from the PEF Endowment Fund. Co-chairs of the Giving Campaign Catie Osborn and Kim Hunter added their thoughts and thanks on the record-breaking gift. “This incredible achievement is only possible because of the generosity of our community,” said Osborn, “Our donors make it clear, year after year, that supporting our schools is a shared priority.” “We’re especially proud that 94% of this grant directly funds the people who make Piedmont schools exceptional: our classroom teachers, librarians, paraeducators, classroom aides, intervention specialists, technology coordinators, counselors, nurses, psychologists, athletics staff, and special education professionals,” said Hunter. The impact of that support stretches back decades. “PEF was founded 50 years ago by parents and neighbors who believed that strong schools are the heart of our community,” said PEF Board Chair Bridget Schreiber. “Half a century later, we are still building on that legacy, and this grant is a powerful example of what we can accomplish together.” That spirit of celebration continues this fall. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Art department will open an art fundraiser today, in collaboration with Piedmont artist Will Mouat. The Piedmont dad created a cartoon poster map of Piedmont, and the sale of each giclee 24”x36” archival print will be donated to the school’s art program. Mouat’s piece compiles dozens of culture icons representing the City of Piedmont and everything within sight from the top of Blair Avenue. The piece captures Piedmont’s landmarks and popular annual events, including the 4th of July Parade, the Turkey Trot, and the Scout Tree Lot. The piece contains details of individual homes and neighbors’ parked vehicles to create a cultural snapshot of Piedmont. “I didn’t really make it to sell,” said Mouat. “I made it because I wanted my kids to have something.” Mouat, a resident for 12 years, started the piece with paper and pencil, moved to ink, then digitized the piece to do the coloring with an iPad. Work on the iPad alone required more than 80 hours of coloring and 80,000 brush strokes. “It’s as if you’re at the top of the hill looking down. It took a lot of mental gymnastics since that’s the wrong angle, but I really wanted SF in the background,” said Mouat. This is the first printing of Mouat’s art piece, and he will have the original on display this weekend in Piedmont Park at both the annual Car Show on Saturday and the Harvest Festival on Sunday. “Our goal is to raise at least $3000 to cover the cost of tuning one kiln and replacing the other,” said Piedmont High School Art Department chair Gillian Bailey. Donors of $150 or more to the PHS Art Materials Fund will receive a hand signed giclee print poster while helping fund art materials for the art department. Prints will be custom printed at East Bay Giclee, a local printer, and should be ready in November. The fundraiser will continue until October 5. With the sale of 20 posters, the Art Department can replace their Ceramics kiln, which broke last week and will be more expensive to repair than replace. New Ceramics teacher Sarah Houchin and her students would benefit greatly from working equipment. Donations will support students in Ceramics 1,2,3,4 and AP 3D Design. articles.text: The city hosted a ribbon cutting at the new Coaches Field batting cages on Friday, Aug. 29, to commemorate the completion of the project. Mayor Andersen joined Eagle Scout candidate Sammy Ragones and the Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation (PBSF) to celebrate. Ragones planned, organized, led and managed the project as his Eagle Scout Service Project, a requirement to become an Eagle Scout, the highest rank in Scouting. He first approached Recreation Director Chelle Putzer in 2023 about rebuilding the old, undersized batting cages. With support and a fundraising offer from PBSF, the project went to the Recreation Commission, Budget Advisory Committee, and then the City Council, which allocated $50,000 in the 2024–25 city budget to replace and expand the cages. Ragones organized Scouts from Troop 15 to dismantle the original cage in December 2024. Public Works managed construction of the new cages in March, which included grading work to expand the footprint and installing electrical power for pitching machines. Ragones then returned to install new nets and turf, completing the project with a plaque recognizing all partners. With two lanes, the new cages now have double the practice capacity. Mayor Andersen and Ragones both spoke at the ceremony. Ragones reminisced about his 10 years playing baseball with PBSF, beginning in kindergarten, and shared that one of his best memories was winning the Bronco championship at Coaches Field. In her remarks, Mayor Andersen called the new cages “an example of the best of a public-private partnership,” and thanked Ragones, the PBSF Board, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich, Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, and community donors, who contributed $20,000 to augment city funding. “Because of this support, Coaches Field now has the nicest batting cages for miles in any direction, open to all members of our extended community,” she said. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team traveled to Hidden Valley Park in Martinez for the 40th annual Ed Sias Invitational on Saturday, September 13. Competing in the small school’s category, the girls’ team placed fourth of 23 schools while the boys were 11th of 24. “The varsity girls’ team had a very good team performance on Saturday in a more competitive field than they faced the previous weekend,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “Once again, the close distance between the first and 5th runner continues to be their strength. “ The boys’ team was missing lead runner Sebastien Swain, and senior captains Noah Sohn and Alex Schleuning. The girls’ team finished equal on points with third place Las Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ team placed fourth of 23 schools at the Ed Sias Invitational. Pictured are Mara Kemp-Malone (left), Leighton Mand, Skylar Best, Amalia Gray, Nikita Gorelik, Viviane Oesterer, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. Lomas at 139, but were narrowly edged out when factoring in the Knights’ sixth runner. Leighton Mand led Piedmont’s girls, placing 19th of 158 runners. Ian Chung (1559) led the boys’ team. He was 56th out of 168 runners. “We were reminded of the importance of every member of a squad. Our top five girls actually tied Las Lomas for third, but their sixth runner was two spots ahead of Nikita Gorelik, which gave them the edge,” Zirkelbach said. Piedmont’s best five runners finished within 38 seconds of each other. Leighton Mand led the way, placing 19th of 158 athletes, recording a time of 13:15 on the two-mile course. Behind Mand was Skylar Best in 29th, clocking a time of 13:29.4. Junior Amalia Gray was 33rd in 13:43.2, while Viviane Oesterer was right behind her in 34th, 13:45.8. Cora Brozowski Schrader rounded out their best five in 38th, 13:52.5. PHS’ sixth runner was Nikita Gorelik, clocking a 14:13.5 to finish 53rd. Boys’ team The PHS boys finished in the top half of the field despite being without top runners like Noah Sohn and Alex Schleuning, while former honorable mention for Athlete of the Year Sebastien Swain misses time as he recovers from surgery. A batch of underclassmen helped. Sophomores Ian Chung placed 56th of 168 runners with a time of 11:31, and classmate Aaron Bennett crossed the line at the same time in 57th in 11:31.3. Dylan Wallway, a freshman, was 66th in 11:42.9. Devon Thai was 73rd, clocking a 11:50.9, while Luca LaForte rounded out Piedmont’s best five in 102nd in 12:33.6. “Devon Thai beat his time on the course from last year by 25 seconds, and Aaron Bennett had a massive improvement of 2:31 over his time on this course as a freshman last year,” Zirkelbach said. Both Wallway and LaForte made their varsity debuts. “Luca LaForte and Dylan Wallway were brought up to run on the varsity team, and both of them ran well in their debut varsity appearances. Luca had a 41-second improvement from his 2024 race time,” Zirkelbach said. articles.text: Before arriving to the hall of Piedmont High for the fall semester, senior Robyn Kim put together a monumental summer. Back on July 7 in Las Vegas, Kim won the U.S. Powerlifting National Championship in the Age 16-17 category at 123 pounds. Kim hit a combined total of 683.4 pounds, including 253.5 pounds in the squat, 132.2 pounds on the bench press, and 297.6 pounds on the dead lift. Her total beat her opponent, Arlete Ruiz Lara, by over 120 pounds. Like many competitive lifters her age, Kim learned about the sport after finding a passion for weightlifting. Kim grew up playing soccer, and competed on Piedmont High’s track and field team in the discus last spring. During the pandemic she and her family built up a collection of weights in their house. After noticing her ability improving, Robyn realized she was getting strong enough to enter the competitive field. “I started lifting during COVID. My dad got a set of weights randomly and they sat around for a little while. I saw a video of the women’s Olympic weightlifting team and it looked really cool. I was inspired to start lifting,” Kim said. “Eventually, I started to see some progress and I was getting stronger. After maybe six or seven months, I became more focused on training and found a structured routine,” she added. Moving from her at-home gym to the YMCA in Oakland, Kim’s workouts began having more structure. “As I started seeing more progress, I realized I had to be more thorough about it. articles.text: Henderson leads Highlanders with 4 touchdowns Piedmont’s football team captured its first win of the season, beating the visiting Berean Christian Eagles 45-12 for their home opener at Witter Field. The Highlanders were coming off back-to-back losses to Salesian and Middletown where they were in tightly contested games in the third quarter before falling behind in the fourth. This time Piedmont kept the gas pedal down for all four quarters. The previous week, PHS last lost to Middletown 34-17, which the Eagles opened their season against in a 22-14 victory. For coach Jordan Seiden and his players, it felt like Piedmont finally put everything together. “The offense got things going, and most importantly, the defense got it together. They were tackling much better and they had better communication. It was one of those games where every player on the roster contributed,” Seiden said. It was a big evening for Xavier Henderson, who scored four touchdowns. “Xavier had a big game. He’s a ball player. In Piedmont, not a lot of kids grow up playing football and it’s a big teaching process. Xavier has played football since he was five or six, so it’s second nature to him. When he’s in his prime shape, he’s one of the best players in the Bay Area. There may be people who are bigger and faster than him, but his instincts, his nose for the ball, and skill set is great,” Seiden said. Junior running back Rehan Rehan Mumtaz scored on a 30-yard touchdown run. Photos by Sajid Mumtaz Xavier Henderson (right) and Dash Waters Worthen celebrate a touchdown. Henderson scored four times against Berean Christian. Mumtaz also had a solid game, scoring on a 30-yard touchdown early in the fourth quarter. “Rehan Mumtaz had the first 100-yard game of his career and scored his second touchdown. He’s incredibly fast and tends to rely on his speed, Seiden said. Seiden has also been impressed by kicker Mattias Seelenberger who converted a 37-yard field goal in the third quarter, while pinpointing a wellplaced kickoff which led to a recovery by Piedmont. “Our kicker made a 37-yard field goal. He’s three for three on field goals and 10 for 10 on PAT attempts. We recovered a kickoff and we’ve always put a heavy emphasis on special teams,” Seiden said. Game Recap After recovering a fumbled snap at the 50-yard line, Piedmont drove six plays to the end zone. On their first play, Mumtaz took a reverse 19 yards to the BC 32, while Jimmy Lagios found Jack Meyjes on a 28-yard reception to the five. After a five-yard penalty, Henderson broke two tackles on a 10-yard touchdown run—making it 7-0 around the 8:50 mark in the first quarter. Henderson scored again on an 18-yard touchdown reception on a screen play at the very end of the first quarter. Berean Christian got one back on a long touchdown pass on fourth down early in the second quarter, making it 14-6 after a botched extra point. After Jason Shum recorded an interception, Piedmont drove to the 14 yard line before Henderson shed another couple of tackles on his way to the end zone, bringing their lead to 21-6 midway through the second quarter. Near the end of the second quarter, quarterback Jimmy Lagios found Jack Meyjes for a 27-yard touchdown pass down the sideline, 28-6. After George Saunders intercepted a pass early in the third, Piedmont drove seven plays to score, capping off with a one-yard touchdown by Henderson for a 35-6 lead. Seelenberger later hit a 37-yard field goal to make it 38-6. After BCHS scored early in the fourth quarter, Piedmont’s final touchdown came on a 30-yard touchdown carry by Mumtaz. articles.text: Staff Photos Allyson Huyhn lands one of her eight kills against Lick-Wilmerding. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team is on a roll, capturing two wins in the past week to create a three-match winning streak. They have improved their record to 6-3. The Highlanders recently beat Lick-Wilmerding in a clean 3-0 sweep at Binks Rawlings Gym on Thursday, September 11. They also defeated Urban in San Francisco 3-1 two days earlier. The results mean Piedmont has now doubled last year’s win total after just nine matches. “We’re young, but we have confidence. It’s had a domino effect on the entire team in the best way possible,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. It’s a night and day difference than previous years. With 11 matches remaining in the regular season, the Highlanders are one win away from matching their win total in 2023, and five wins away from the last time the team qualified for the North Coast Section playoffs in 2018. “The connection between all the girls is just insane this year,” stated senior Stella Wilk. “We’re all really putting in the work and you’re seeing all the work in practice coming through in games.” “When I first played on varsity as a sophomore, I looked up to all the older girls. This year, we’re really young so it’s exciting to see them bring the energy,” added senior Mira Sachs. 3-0 over Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont won its clean sweep by scores of 25-16, 25-14, and 25-13. In the first set, the Highlanders dominated with 10 kills, taking advantage of the Tigers’ offensive and defensive errors. Sofia Meyer led the way with four, while, Wilk, Maika Ting, and Allyson Huyhn had two each. The second set was even more one-sided with 16 kills to their credit, allowing many starters to rest in the third set. Ting landed five spikes, Izara Dando had four, Sachs had three, Huyhn and Wilk had two, while Jasmine Houlder had one. In the third set, Lick-Wilmerding actually kept it a close contest at 12-8, but Piedmont only allowed five more points from then on. articles.text: Coach Jordan Seiden was named head coach of Piedmont varsity football in 2022, taking over at a time when the program’s future was in doubt. He brought more than 25 years of coaching experience, having led teams at Skyline High School in Oakland, Capuchino High School in San Bruno, and Castro Valley High School. With deep roots in local gridiron history, he has made it his mission to restore Highlander pride through leadership grounded in hard work, respect, and camaraderie. Since his arrival, coach Seiden has led a remarkable turnaround. Piedmont football was on the brink of collapse after COVID decimated participation and raised questions about the future of the program. Under his leadership, the team has rebounded with renewed pride and energy, climbing back to win back-toback league titles. A Bay Area native, coach Seiden played at St. Mary’s High School and graduated from Berkeley High in 1991. He continued his football journey at Diablo Valley College and UC Davis before studying kinesiology at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. Off the field, coach Seiden has devoted his career to supporting young people in challenging situations. He worked at Alameda County’s juvenile hall and later with the Oakland Unified School District, helping students stay in school or return after time away. For him, the true measure of success is helping young people grow into responsible citizens as well as athletes. Coach Seiden continues to inspire players, families, and the wider community with a vision built around discipline, teamwork, respect, and lasting Highlander pride. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company (MTC) is extending its run of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day, now ending on September 28. The play is set at the Eureka Day School in Berkeley, California, portrayed as a “bastion of progressive ideals with a board of directors that values inclusion above all else.” The majority of the play takes place during meetings between parents and administrators concerning requirements for vaccination after an outbreak of mumps at the school. These meetings prompt school leadership to reconsider its liberal vaccine policy in comedic and dramatic ways. The New York Times called Eureka Day and Jonathan Spector’s “lively portrait of a debate over mandatory vaccinations” as the “the perfect play for our age of disagreement.” MTC’s production of Eureka Day is presented in partnership with Aurora Theatre Company, where the play had its world premiere in 2018, two years before the COVID-19 pandemic and the discourse over required vaccinations that followed. Marin Theatre Company’s production features nearly all its original cast members from the 2018 world premiere. The cast includes Howard Swain as Don, Lisa Anne Porter as Suzanne, Leontyne MbeleMbong as Carina, Charisse Loriaux as Meiko, Teddy Spencer as Eli, and Kelsey Sloan as Winter. Eureka Day features assistant direction by Molly Aaronson-Gel, scenic design by Richard Olmsted, costume design by Maggie Whittaker, lighting design by Jeff Rowlings, sound design by Ray Archie, and video content by Teddy Hulsker. Nick Carvalho is the stage manager with Mona Jean Ortiz as Assistant Stage Manager A pre-show presentation from MTC’s stage designer is held on Thursday, September 18. Eureka Day is appropriate for audience members 14 and older. Visit https://purchase.marintheatre.org/EventAvailability?EventId=49801 to purchase tickets. Cast of Eureka Day

articles.text: Smuin Ballet Company presents its fall season, entitled “Extremely Close,” on September 19 and 20 at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. Smuin’s 32nd season is directed by Amy Seiwert and is inspired by Alejandro Cerrundo’s art installation and movement drama Extremely Close, set to a score by Philip Glass and Dustin O’Halloran. Fall performances include the West Coast premiere of choreographer Justin Peck’s Partita, set to Caroline Shaw’s Pulitzer Prize-winning “Partita for 8 Voices,” a unique number featuring eight dancers in sneakers. Smuin Ballet will be the first company outside of New York City Ballet to perform the work since it premiered in 2022. The final piece being performed in this season’s fall programming is A Long Night choreographed by Seiwert, a former mentee of the late Michael Smuin. Seiwert reimagines Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream with humor and heartfelt storytelling that honors George Balanchine’s original choreography. A Long Night premiered in 2023 for BalletX in Philadelphia and is set to songs by Patsy Cline, Pink Martini, Harry Nilsson, and more. “To have Justin’s [Peck] and Alejandro’s [Cerrundo] work in my first curated season is an honor and a thrill,” said Seiwert. “Justin’s creative path reminds me a bit of our founder Michael Smuin’s. His work in film and on Broadway informs the distinctive style he brings to his creations for the concert dance stage. And Alejandro’s work exemplifies how extraordinary contemporary dance can be: musical and theatrical, with a mystery that will take your breath away.” Smuin Ballet hosts two performances at Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek September 19 through 20: Friday at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. The company’s fall season concludes at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts in San Francisco September 26 through October 5 with eight performances scheduled: Friday, September 26 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday and Sunday, September 27 and 28 at 2 p.m.; Thursday, October 2 at 7:30 p.m.; Friday, October 3 at 7:30 p.m.; Saturday, October 4 at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.; and Sunday, October 5 at 2 p.m. Single-day tickets are available at www.smuinballet.org. She is charged with killing Chase Andrews (Taylor John-Smith), a popular young man from a wealthy and prominent family. Her defense counsel is retired attorney, Tom Milton (David Strathairn), who has known Kya since she was a child and is committed to her innocence. The tale is told in a series of flashbacks, beginning with Kya as a young girl who lives on the edge of a stretching marsh with her mother, siblings, and abusive, drunken father. After a violent episode, her mother, suitcase in hand, silently walks away, soon to be followed by her brother and sisters, and Kyra finds herself left with her father. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, September 17, 2025 The Musical Gourmet Music and athletics By Joseph Gold The world of music is a very competitive place - overt and covert. In reality, the two terms are rather similar. Competition is intense. Musicians are athletes of the arts. Timing is imperative and stamina is also. The general public does not realize how much energy it takes to play a concert. Think of a concert as a musical marathon. The performer needs nuanced musical abilities in combination with complete and total concentration. The public enjoys experiencing perfection. In the past, it was the music that was important. Now an ostentatious display has usurped integrity. Classical musicians have adopted the superficial world of the pop music scene. Famous ballet dancers like Rudolf Nureyev were incredible athletes. Can you imagine how good a ballet dancer Romanian gymnast Nadia Comaneci would have been had she so desired? Interestingly enough, both ballet dancers and gymnasts use professional choreographers. Their music is selected with great care. Opera singers have always been very popular with the public. They are generally known by their excessive girth given that the only exercise they do is eatThe Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet ing. But don’t be fooled. Singing on the opera stage is very physically taxing. Star concert performers must keep themselves in good shape physically. Local violinist Stuart Canin has had an amazing career. He is almost 100 years old and has continued to play well into his late 90s in admirable style. Yehudi Menuhin has always practiced yoga. Another violin prodigy from San Francisco was Ruggiero Ricci. He could have been an outstanding gymnast on the parallel bars. Guys I know who served with him in the army said that he could do chin-ups with great rapidity and ease. Violinist Jascha Heifetz competed in tennis, table tennis and pistol shooting. The greatest players always kept themselves an excellent physical shape. It was also a pleasure to learn their philosophy. They believed that the musical score was the most important thing. As interpreters, they were at the service of the music. Things are very different now. Conductors have lived long lives. Their form of exercise is very much like aerobics. Sincerity should also figure as a very important aspect of music. The virtuoso musician makes things look easy and effortless. Given that technique is the cornerstone of any art, nuance must come into play. Despite all the superficialities that we see from “superstar” musicians, the rules of music are very simple. The great American musician Albert Spalding stated it as: “sincerity, sincerity, sincerity.“ I have always admired football coach Vince Lombardi. Can you imagine him as a conductor of an orchestra? He would have been marvelous. He espoused sincerity and respect in every way. He saw the entire picture and conveyed it to his teams. But in reality, “the team that controls, the line of scrimmage wins the game.” That’s the way it should be in music. Violinist Joseph Gold as a young man on the USC wrestling team. articles.text: How deep pressure therapy from a service dog can improve mental health The psychiatric service dog has emerged as a potentially effective way to manage stress, despite being one of the least pioneered innovations in mental health. Although emotional support animals were banned from traveling in cabins outside carriers, the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 allows service dogs trained to actively mitigate disabilities full public access. These disabilities can be visible or invisible. One task psychiatric service dogs can perform is deep pressure therapy, which involves more than just a dog laying on its owner. To effectively perform this task, the dog must be trained to tighten its core to maintain balance while dropping its weight onto the owner. This requires impressive stamina, as well as intense focus on the handler. Deep pressure therapy can be incredibly effective for individuals struggling with anxiety, depression, ADHD, obsessive, compulsive disorder (OCD), and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The dog acts as a weighted blanket, providing calming and grounding pressure that can lift mood, decrease anxiety, increase focus, and stabilize the handler. Despite skeptics who claim the dog is merely laying there for comfort, service dogs trained for deep pressure therapy actively respond to specific cues to legitimately aid their handler. Many people assume they don’t qualify for a service dog due to their invisible or seemingly minor disability. However, a service dog can greatly improve quality of life, even with a simple task like deep pressure therapy. Pairing this task with alert task training may decrease the need for psychotherapy sessions, reduce dependency on psychiatric medication, and even help handlers wean off long-term medication entirely. As a holistic approach to addressing the mental health epidemic, psychiatric service dogs offer a promising solution. With increased stress affecting many lives, deep pressure therapy from a trained service dog could provide much-needed relief. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. The Wednesday before, the group enjoyed a historical tour led by Nancy DeRoche through her neighborhood above Oakland Avenue. The highlight was the Blair Avenue house where Jack London wrote The Call of the Wild in 1902–03. In about 1910, the house was moved two lots up the street to make way for the Sutro Mansion — a reminder of how homes were once relocated by rolling them across logs pulled by horses, mules, or oxen. While common a century ago, such methods would not be permitted under today’s regulations. Built in 1879 by Hugh Craig, it is the city’s second-oldest residence and a large Stick Italianate Victorian that remains striking even today. He purchased five acres in Piedmont and built his home in 1879 on Vernal (now Highland) Avenue. Following the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, many families relocated across the Bay, swelling the populations of Oakland and Piedmont. articles.text: A record turnout of 26 readers showed up at Piedmont Community Center in Piedmont Park on September 8 for the First Mondays Reading Group discussion. Participating were Sue Backer, Sarah Johnson, Bill Ahern, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Ken Young, Mike Henn, Karin Fetherston, Heidi Schmidt, Laura Goldman, Peggy Shultz, Hilary Honore, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Pat McMahon, Nancy Henn, Adrienne Hamlin, Alicia Rivera, Martin Levy, Orrel Lanter, Gerry Gregg, Darby Gregg, Linda Sigel, Mary Carter, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased to have Rose Byrne with them for the first time. The group was there to talk about The Women by Kristin Hannah, an author of more than 20 historical fiction novels. Hannah’s books are known for their character development, historical depth, and themes of love, loss, and female friendship. Her best-selling work, The Nightingale, has sold over 4.5 million copies worldwide and has been published in 45 languages. The Women is Hannah’s most recent novel. It was published in 2024 and tells the story of Frances “Frankie” McGrath, a privileged, young woman who defies her conservative parents to become an Army nurse during the Vietnam War. The book debuted at number one on The New York Times fiction best-seller list, was at number one for 10 weeks, and was one of the most borrowed titles in American public libraries at the time. It’s the story of Frankie’s incredibly hard nursing experiences in Vietnam, the deep bonds she forms with other nurses, and her difficult return to an America where the sacrifices and trauma of its returning female veterans were not understood or appreciated. In January 2024, Warner Bros acquired the book’s screen rights for a film adaptation, and a movie is in the works. The Women generated a lot of First Mondays Reading Group discussion. Some members of the group had many issues with the book and even questioned whether it was “serious literature.” The story seemed like a soap opera with one horribly bad thing after another happening to Frankie. One reader wondered if any character could be less innocent. The group believed that the issues Frankie experienced did happen to those involved in the Vietnam war, but was it possible for all these problems to happen to one person? Some readers felt that “the bones of the book” were good, but the storytelling was so “flowery” that they were turned off. The war experiences packed into the first part of the book seemed like a MASH television episode, but they weren’t funny. Dead men coming back into Frankie’s life was almost expected by the readers. For some of them it became silly. Many readers were also disappointed with the story’s hard to believe ending, For one male reader this was “a book by a woman, about women, for women.” Some readers would have preferred a non-fiction history of peoples’ real Vietnam War experiences rather than this fiction. Readers felt The Women missed an opportunity to tell the tragic story of this war more credibly. Additionally, the book at 470 pages seemed long. However, some readers had more positive things to say about the book. They felt they got a lot out of the novel. It brought back their Vietnam experiences, many of which were hard. The book generated memories and provoked emotions that are important for people, and especially younger people, to understand. Additionally, Hannah’s message that there is a lack of understanding and appreciation of women’s contributions during the Vietnam War is an important one. Another enjoyable part of the discussion was the readers sharing their different experiences during this Vietnam War period. This conversation took on a life of its own and it was interesting to hear how people wanted to contribute in different ways based on their motivations and consciences during the war. The readers had to be reminded to come back to talk about the book. The group seemed to accept that The Women has flaws but it does address an important historical issue regarding the lack of understanding of the role of women in the Vietnam War. The group had previously selected The Wright Brothers by David McCullough for October’s read and Euphoria by Lily King for their November book. After Dick Carter’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates, the readers chose Differ We Must by Steve Inskeep for their December read. With all their business done, they took a group photo in the circle outside the Community Hall. The group will meet on the patio outside the Community Hall in Piedmont Park on October 6th at 1:30 PM for their next discussion. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https://bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call the Recreation Department at 510 420-3070, to register. articles.text: [From August 2022] Hola! Lisbon, Portugal is a great city for walking and hiking. The streets are tightly packed together with rolling hills similar to San Francisco, where you can find great food, culture, warm weather, and a lot of history. Should you ever find yourself in Lisboa, an easy walk for all ages goes straight through the heart of the city from Parque Eduardo VII, down Avenida da Liberdade and Rau Augusta to the historic Praça do Comércio and edge of the Tagus River for just 2.1 miles of walking. The route from Praça do Comércio, or Commerce Square, goes slightly uphill on its way to Park Eduardo VII, so we start our venture at the top at the park for an easy point A-B-C walk. Parque Eduardo VII is 64 acres and just north of Avenida da Liberdad. The park is named after King Edward VII of Great The trail goes down Avenida da Liberdad, which has several monuments like this one to Antonio Feliciano De Castillo, a famous writer from the 1800s. After Avenida da Liberdad (walking from Parque Eduardo VII) is Monumento aos Restauradores. The path leads to Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV. One of the most visited locations in Lisboa (native pronunciation), is Commerce Square with its large monument to King Jose I.

Britain after he visited Portugal in 1903 to strengthen the relationship between the two countries and reaffirm their alliance. articles.text: This fall, Stagebridge—Oakland’s pioneering center for creative aging—is inviting older adults back for another season of classes that spark curiosity, laughter, and connection. Beginning the week of September 22, the schedule includes everything from storytelling and acting to dance, improv, and clowning. Stagebridge has long believed that staying active and engaged is key to thriving in later years. Science agrees: picking up new skills and keeping socially connected can improve memory, boost mood, and even support physical health. But the real magic shows up in the community itself. Toby, a Stagebridge teacher who recently returned after some time away, described the experience this way: “I had such a wonderful time with my cohort. They were openhearted, delightful, funny, poetic, and kind—and did I mention FUNNY? When I first walked back into the church, I felt a whiff of sadness, missing my great clown sister Joan Mankin. But that soon dissolved into pure joy when the actual magic of Stagebridge took over. All I know is you have an enchanted island there, one where I made fantastic new friends and reconnected with old ones.” For many, that sense of “enchanted island” is what makes Stagebridge unique. Students come not only to learn but also to find camaraderie, to reconnect with creativity, and to share in the humor and wisdom that flourish in later life. Teachers, many of whom are artists still active in the Bay Area, bring both skill and heart to their work, creating spaces where every participant feels welcome. A quick look at Stagebridge’s event calendar shows how alive this community really is, from performances to storytelling nights that bring members together both in and beyond the classroom. Interested in joining the fun? Learn more about Stagebridge and all upcoming fall classes at www.stagebridge.org. Stagebridge is America’s oldest performing arts nonprofit for older adults. Based in Oakland, CA | www.stagebridge.org | info@stagebridge.org | (510) 210-3773 Stagebridge Summer Camp: where bold costumes meet even bolder personalities. When the rhythm hits, the feet don’t stop—Stagebridge keeps the beat alive.

articles.text: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has a list of 20 common fraud schemes on its “Scams and Safety”1 web page, including credit card theft. The thief makes small purchases with your stolen credit card number and sees if they go through, if they do, then they hit your account for bigger purchases. You should have an email, text message, or phone alert set up with your credit card company, so that the bank will contact you if there are any unusual spending items, if there are illegitimate charges, you must report to the bank as soon as possible so you won’t be charged for those items. The bank will lock your account and send you a new card in the mail. This can be frustrating when you have set up monthly withdrawals to be charged against your card. You’ll have to go to those companies’ websites and change the card numbers you use for those charges. How to protect yourself from Internet scams and fraudulent schemes. The FBI says protect your computer2 by keeping systems and software up to date and install a strong reputable anti-virus program. Also, ou will pay a yearly fee for antivirus, antispyware, and firewall software services, but the safety they provide makes it well worth the cost. Another way to protect yourself is by regularly visiting the Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC’s)4 website for updated information and warnings. articles.text: The thought of moving from your Piedmont home can stir a mix of emotions. This is where you’ve celebrated milestones, raised children, and built your story. But for many, the next chapter isn’t about loss—it’s about opportunity. Imagine waking up to sweeping Bay views, joining friends for a morning round of golf, or savoring a chef-prepared dinner without lifting a finger. The Bay Area has a remarkable selection of communities designed to make your next stage as rich and fulfilling as your last. • Rossmoor – In the heart of Walnut Creek, this 55+ gated community offers resort-style amenities, from championship golf to cultural clubs. • Merrill Gardens – Oakland living with modern style, flexible support, and a vibrant activities program. • Piedmont Gardens – A lush, full-service community with everything from independent living to skilled nursing—plus proximity to local dining and culture. • St. Paul’s Towers – Sophisticated high-rise living above Lake Merritt with full care services and city life at your doorstep. • Coterie Cathedral Hill – San Francisco’s most luxurious senior residence, blending high design, fine dining, and worldclass wellness programs. I understand the hesitation— downsizing is a big step. It’s more than just finding a new home; it’s sorting through decades of belongings, making big decisions, and managing the logistics. That’s why I’ve built a network of trusted senior service providers—from estate sale experts to professional organizers—who can handle every step with care. For many, the move brings unexpected benefits: freedom from home maintenance, a built-in social network, and the peace of mind that comes from knowing support is available if needed. This isn’t about giving up your life. It’s about elevating it. If you’re thinking about making a change, I’d be happy to introduce you to my Senior Living Consultant, who can help you discover a home that truly fits your needs and lifestyle. Downsizing could be the start of a more peaceful, manageable chapter— where your home works for you and every day feels a little lighter. Dear MacMama, I know this is the time of year when new iPhones come out. I have an iPhone 13. Do you think this is a good time to upgrade? I really enjoy the camera on my iPhone and I understand that the new ones have much better cameras. I love to take photographs not only of my family but of flowers and landscapes. So which one would you recommend for me? Ellen, Rockridge Dear Ellen, I think this is an excellent time to upgrade. There are four versions of the iPhone 17, and I’ll give you a quick description of each. If the camera is most important, I’d recommend the iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max. At this writing, all are available for pre-order and should be in Apple stores on Friday, Sept. 19. If you order now, expect a wait of several weeks—new iPhones usually take six to eight weeks before supply catches up. All models include Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is three times more scratch-resistant, and the new Center Stage front camera that can shoot with both front and rear cameras simultaneously. • iPhone 17: The “basic” model isn’t basic at all. It comes in five colors and features a 48-megapixel dual fusion camera with .5x, 1x, and 2x zoom. Apple claims all-day battery life. It should be 50% faster than your iPhone 13, with a 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR display. Prices range from $799 (256 GB) to $999 (512 GB). • iPhone 17 Air: New this year, this is the thinnest iPhone yet at 5.6 mm, with a 6.5-inch titanium body. It has a 48-megapixel main camera and up to 2x zoom, but fewer features than the Pro models. It’s designed for people who want a sleek, futuristic look. Available in four colors, it ranges from $999 (256 GB) to $1,399 (1 TB). • iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max: If photography is your priority, these are the ones. Both have forged aluminum bodies and three 48-megapixel rear cameras, including a new telephoto with up to 8x optical zoom. They support ProRes Raw video and offer the best battery life yet. The Pro has a 6.3-inch display and costs $1,099 to $1,499. The Pro Max, at 6.9 inches, has even more features and a new 2 TB option, ranging from $1,199 to $1,999. Each phone serves a different audience: • The iPhone 17 offers strong performance at a lower price. • The Air is for those who prize design and portability. • The Pro and Pro Max deliver professional-quality photos, longer battery life, and expanded storage. Apple also introduced new watches and AirPods Pro 3. A notable feature is live translation in beta, currently supporting English, French, German, Portuguese, and Spanish, with more languages coming soon. Remember: you can trade in your old iPhone, finance with the Apple Card at no interest, or use Apple’s yearly upgrade program. Carriers will also launch promotions starting Sept. 19. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional who provides Apple consultation and troubleshooting in homes and offices. Contact her at 510-520-7760, cookie@themacmama.com, or www.themacmama.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department is inviting community members to kick off the Harvest Festival weekend by joining for a park screening of Migration (2023). The movie starts at 7:15 p.m. in Piedmont Park, though families can arrive as early as 6:30 p.m. to enjoy food and reserve a spot for a blanket on the lawn. A Canasta Kitchen food truck will be at the event, ready to take orders by 6:30 p.m. Migration is an animated movie that follows a family of mallard ducks who try to convince their overprotective father to go on a spectacular vacation as they migrate from New England, through New York City, to Jamaica. This month’s Movie in the Park is sponsored by Piedmont Cub Scouts. Families enjoy a Movie in the Park screening on the Piedmont Park lawn. For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
